title: Revision Receipts
user: A secondary-school or college writing teacher who needs to give a class useful feedback and see whether a student acted on it without reading every draft side by side.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A teacher explicitly asks how others scale writing feedback, weighing tools against manual feedback.
JabRef users request a diff view before committing changes, a parallel request for a clear review artifact before a change becomes final.

recurrence: A direct 2026 classroom request and a separate high-friction review workflow request point to the same missing artifact: an explainable before/after change view. Feedback load is acute at assignment deadlines.
current_workaround: Teachers leave comments in Google Docs/Word, students resubmit, and teachers manually hunt for which suggestions were adopted.
incumbents_and_gap: Google Docs, Microsoft Word, and Grammarly offer comments and generic diffs; they do not turn selected teacher comments into a student-owned, concise revision receipt for a class roster.
smallest_useful_product: A browser-based document-pair tool: teacher marks 1–3 feedback goals, student uploads a revised plain-text/Markdown draft, and the tool produces quoted changed passages plus a student reflection. Non-goals: generating prose, plagiarism detection, grading, or an LMS.
success_measure: In a four-week pilot, a teacher can verify adoption of two feedback goals per student in under two minutes and at least 70% of students submit a receipt.
monetization: free — local/exportable files are crucial for classroom trust; a paid roster workspace could be tested only after adoption.
constraints: No model-generated writing or hidden scoring; files should remain in-browser by default; disclose that textual change is not proof of learning.
why_distinct: The unit of value is evidence that feedback changed a draft, not another AI writing assistant or document editor.

title: Kind Recall
user: An adult language learner who wants vocabulary to become usable in conversation without punitive streak mechanics.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker says learners forget words despite months of streaks, flashcards, and progress bars, and asks what makes vocabulary stick long term.
Anki users request a streak feature for motivation, while the issue explicitly notes that missed-day streaks can become toxic.

recurrence: Two independent learner-tool communities surface the motivation-versus-retention tension; the Anki request had 17 reactions. The pain recurs daily but is most visible after a lapse.
current_workaround: Use Anki/Quizlet/Duolingo streaks, set reminders, and hope that repeated recognition becomes recall in real situations.
incumbents_and_gap: Anki offers powerful scheduling and Duolingo offers engagement; neither makes recovery after a missed week a first-class, non-shaming workflow anchored in the learner's own sentences.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA for 20–100 user-entered words: schedule short typed or spoken recall prompts in personal contexts, show a forgiving return queue after lapses, and record confidence separately from correctness. Non-goals: a language course, content marketplace, or chatbot.
success_measure: After 30 days, 50% of weekly active learners return after one missed week and improve delayed free-recall accuracy by 15 percentage points on their own word set.
monetization: one-time — a personal offline study utility should not make retention dependent on an ongoing subscription.
constraints: Keep decks and recordings on device; no claims of clinical efficacy; speech checking must be optional and never rank accents.
why_distinct: It treats lapse recovery and context-rich production as the product, instead of adding gamification to flashcards.

title: Plainspoken Drills
user: A privacy-conscious language learner who wants interactive listening and speaking drills without generative-AI accounts or cloud conversation recording.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A learner asks for interactive language apps/sites specifically excluding LLMs/GenAI because the established services have adopted it.
AnkiDroid documents a real Android text-to-speech failure where locale-only selection chooses an unavailable voice rather than an installed one.

recurrence: The direct request and a separate mobile-learning accessibility failure show that dependable device-native audio remains a practical unmet need, not merely a preference debate.
current_workaround: Use mainstream apps despite data concerns, play downloaded audio manually, or assemble Anki cards and Android TTS settings themselves.
incumbents_and_gap: Duolingo, Babbel, and AI conversation apps require accounts and increasingly use generative features; Anki is flexible but is not a guided local audio-drill experience.
smallest_useful_product: A no-login Android-first PWA that imports a small CC-licensed phrase pack, plays installed-device TTS/audio, records optional self-playback, and runs branching listen/choose/say drills. Non-goals: open-ended AI conversation, speech grading, or proprietary course content.
success_measure: At least 80% of test users complete a 10-minute drill offline after initial download, and no account/network request is needed for review.
monetization: one-time — users seeking a no-cloud alternative should be able to buy a durable local tool rather than pay with surveillance.
constraints: Use only CC/public-domain phrase packs; respect platform TTS availability; keep recordings local and disclose that pronunciation is not automatically assessed.
why_distinct: It makes non-generative, device-native practice pleasant rather than being a stripped-down clone of an AI tutor.

title: Equation Audio Guide
user: A learner or teacher publishing technical articles with equations and code who needs a correct, reviewable spoken route through the material.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An ESL technical writer asks how to read articles containing code, tables, plots, and equations aloud rather than reading symbols verbatim.
Anki tracks migration/investigation work for MathJax 4, showing that mathematical rendering is an active maintenance concern in a major study tool.

recurrence: A direct 2026 accessibility/learning request and ongoing MathJax work show that technical notation remains hard to move across reading modes.
current_workaround: Skip equations in TTS, write ad-hoc alt text, or listen to poor automatic symbol-by-symbol readings.
incumbents_and_gap: Screen readers and MathJax render notation, while generic TTS reads prose; neither gives authors a compact editable narration script with diagram/table placeholders for a whole article.
smallest_useful_product: Static web editor that accepts Markdown/LaTex, proposes deterministic spoken-math phrases and code-reading chunks, flags ambiguity, and exports an audio-script checklist. Non-goals: synthetic voice hosting, OCR, or solving equations.
success_measure: For ten representative equations, a teacher can approve or correct a narrated script in under 15 minutes and listeners answer 80% of accompanying comprehension checks.
monetization: free — accessible technical publishing benefits from open formats; optional institutional support can fund maintenance.
constraints: Do not claim universal screen-reader equivalence; support MathML/LaTex safely with no arbitrary HTML execution; output must remain editable by a human.
why_distinct: It produces an author-reviewed explanation of notation, rather than wrapping generic TTS around a web page.

title: Self-Study Checkpoints
user: A serious independent math or computer-science learner who needs an externally legible way to prove progress through a difficult topic without enrolling in a full course.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A self-learner of abstract algebra asks how to validate deep study and specifically wishes for a rigorous scheduled examination as an external benchmark.
Anki discusses exposing evaluation for user-provided parameters, reflecting demand for learners to inspect and tune assessment behavior rather than accept opaque defaults.

recurrence: Both sources point to learners needing transparent, intentional assessment. The direct request describes motivation failure without a clear benchmark.
current_workaround: Follow a textbook alone, solve selected exercises, join an expensive course, or publish informal notes without a coherent mastery record.
incumbents_and_gap: Coursera/edX offer whole courses and Brilliant offers guided practice; neither lets an individual assemble a small, rigorous checkpoint plan with publicly reviewable proof attempts and a chosen assessor.
smallest_useful_product: A static-web checkpoint builder: define a syllabus slice, target date, problem set links, proof/code submission prompts, and an invited reviewer rubric; export a signed completion packet. Non-goals: issuing accredited credentials, auto-solving proofs, or proctoring.
success_measure: At least 40% of created checkpoints result in a completed packet reviewed by another person within the chosen 6–12 week window.
monetization: free — credibility depends on portable, inspectable packets rather than a proprietary credential wall.
constraints: Clearly label peer review as non-accredited; link rather than redistribute copyrighted exercises; do not use hidden automated grading for proofs.
why_distinct: It supplies commitment and evidence around self-study, not another content library or AI answer engine.

title: Humane Practical Exams
user: An instructor or training provider assessing practical technical skills who wants credible evidence without invasive remote-proctoring surveillance.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Kubernetes certification candidate reports that extreme remote proctoring made technical competence secondary to fear of normal behaviours being flagged.
A user reports checklist items lost between laptop and phone sessions, illustrating why assessment evidence needs an explicit durable export rather than trust in a cloud workspace.

recurrence: The direct account identifies a high-severity assessment harm; separate cross-device data-loss evidence reinforces the need for portable evidence rather than opaque session monitoring.
current_workaround: Use webcam/room surveillance, locked-down browsers, live screen share, or unstructured take-home work that is difficult to assess consistently.
incumbents_and_gap: Examity/ProctorU optimize surveillance, while GitHub Classroom manages assignments; there is little lightweight tooling for a timed open-book practical that collects an artifact, command history chosen by the candidate, and a transparent rubric.
smallest_useful_product: Self-hostable web app for a timed task brief, local artifact upload, candidate-written work log, checkpoint hashes, and assessor rubric with an exportable assessment record. Non-goals: webcam monitoring, browser lockdown, identity verification, or AI cheating detection.
success_measure: In a pilot, assessors can grade 90% of submissions from the artifact and rubric alone, and fewer than 10% require a surveillance-style follow-up.
monetization: one-time — small training providers need a clear alternative to per-candidate surveillance fees.
constraints: Do not market it as cheat-proof; minimize personally identifiable data; encrypt submissions and implement deletion dates; accessibility accommodations must be configurable.
why_distinct: It makes assessable work visible while deliberately refusing the surveillance features that caused the reported harm.

title: Source Trail Workbook
user: A humanities instructor teaching undergraduates how to research digitally and needing a repeatable exercise that shows search decisions, source quality, and claims.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An instructor asks how to teach digital research workflows to undergraduate philosophy students, explicitly seeking free/open tools and presentation guidance.
JabRef users request support for multiple journal-abbreviation lists, a concrete sign that citation/reference normalization is not one-size-fits-all.

recurrence: A direct 2026 teaching request plus an independent reference-management customization request show that research workflow needs are both pedagogical and discipline-specific.
current_workaround: Demonstrate browser searches live, ask students to submit a bibliography, and use Zotero/JabRef without capturing how sources or claims were selected.
incumbents_and_gap: Zotero and JabRef manage citations, and library guides explain evaluation; neither is a small classroom worksheet that preserves a student's query, rejected result, claim, quote, and citation as one auditable trail.
smallest_useful_product: Offline-first workbook with structured entries for question, query, source metadata, credibility notes, supporting/contradicting quote, and citation export; teachers can distribute a template JSON file. Non-goals: web scraping, AI research answers, or a reference manager replacement.
success_measure: In one assignment, 80% of students submit at least three claim-to-source trails and an instructor can identify unsupported claims without opening a separate bibliography tool.
monetization: free — open access is explicit in the teaching request, and local files reduce institutional adoption friction.
constraints: Do not copy paywalled content; cite source URLs and user-entered short quotations only; support export formats without pretending citation formatting proves source quality.
why_distinct: It teaches the reasoning trail behind research, not merely reference collection or AI-powered search.

title: Code Lesson Replay
user: A remote programming tutor who needs to review a student's reasoning between live sessions without recording an entire screen call.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A prospective instructor tool explicitly asks teachers and tutors about pain points with Zoom, Replit, and VS Code Live Share for remote coding lessons.
A Logseq user reports incomplete rendering in the built-in PDF viewer, a reminder that study/lesson review must preserve the original artifact rather than rely on a fragile rendered view.

recurrence: A direct tutor discovery thread and separate learning-artifact rendering failure highlight a recurring problem: context gets lost between the live explanation and later review.
current_workaround: Record Zoom, ask for a Git commit, use screen shares, or reconstruct what the student tried from a final code snapshot.
incumbents_and_gap: Zoom records too much, VS Code Live Share is synchronous, and Replit shares a workspace; none makes a short student-controlled sequence of run, failure, hypothesis, edit, and result easy to review asynchronously.
smallest_useful_product: VS Code extension that records opt-in command/output and named file diffs into a local replay bundle with student annotations, playable as text by a tutor. Non-goals: remote control, keystroke surveillance, cloud IDE, or automatic code grading.
success_measure: Tutors can identify a student's first wrong hypothesis from a five-minute replay in under three minutes, without a video call recording.
monetization: one-time — independent tutors need a small tool, not another per-seat collaboration subscription.
constraints: Mask secrets and allow per-command exclusion; local bundle by default; never capture webcam/audio or arbitrary keystrokes; use documented VS Code APIs.
why_distinct: It records learning decisions around code, not an always-on screen recording or another online IDE.

title: Objective Loop
user: A self-learner using AI and other materials who needs questions and review scheduling tied to stated learning objectives, rather than a generic chat history.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker wants learning products with spaced repetition/follow-up questions and says ChatGPT does not track what they know or their learning objectives.
Anki documents confusing behaviour from extending daily limits, showing that review scheduling controls can become opaque to learners.

recurrence: A direct request for objective-aware learning plus a mature SRS project's scheduling confusion identify a specific gap: transparent mapping from goal to review, not more generated cards.
current_workaround: Ask a chatbot for quizzes, manually make Anki cards, or use course checklists that do not adapt to demonstrated recall.
incumbents_and_gap: ChatGPT has conversation memory and Anki has scheduling; neither makes a learner-maintained objective tree the visible source of questions, evidence, and next review.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA where users enter objectives and evidence links, attach manually written short-answer prompts, log confidence/correctness, and see a simple explainable next-review queue. Non-goals: LLM card generation, content ingestion, or social feeds.
success_measure: Within two weeks, 60% of active users attach at least one reviewed prompt to three objectives and can explain why every due prompt appeared.
monetization: one-time — the value is durable personal learning data, best kept independent of an AI subscription.
constraints: No opaque recommendation model; local encrypted export; make review calculations inspectable and permit manual overrides.
why_distinct: It connects intentional objectives to recall evidence, instead of being a thin chat wrapper or another card generator.

title: Future Skills Portfolio
user: A parent or home-school educator unsure how to develop a child's math/CS strengths in an AI-rich world and needing concrete, human-reviewable challenges rather than predictions about careers.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A home-schooling parent asks what to teach a mathematically and computationally talented child when AI appears to solve advanced math and coding tasks.
Anki is considering a cross-platform add-on/template system, demonstrating ongoing demand to adapt a learning tool's activities rather than use a fixed curriculum.

recurrence: A direct parent concern and an independent request for adaptable learning templates show that fixed content is a poor response to changing goals. The concern is consequential but emerging.
current_workaround: Continue with standard worksheets/coding courses, follow AI news anxiously, or assemble disconnected projects and competitions.
incumbents_and_gap: Khan Academy, Scratch, and coding platforms supply exercises; they do not help a family curate a portfolio of explanation, modelling, debugging, collaboration, and judgment challenges with a transparent adult rubric.
smallest_useful_product: A printable/static challenge deck for ages 10–16: each card has a build/explain/critique task, material limits, reflection prompts, and a parent/peer rubric; families can create and share local decks. Non-goals: career prediction, AI tutoring, child social network, or data collection.
success_measure: In a six-week family pilot, each child completes four artifacts across at least three skill modes and an adult can cite a concrete growth observation for each artifact.
monetization: one-time — families can buy a curated deck, while the base format remains printable and durable.
constraints: Age-appropriate and offline by default; no child accounts or public profiles; contributors must license challenges for reuse; avoid claims about future employability.
why_distinct: It turns an abstract AI-era anxiety into varied human capabilities demonstrated through artifacts, not an AI course for children.

title: Privacy Class Check-in
user: A teacher running a small class who needs a quick attendance signal but does not want biometrics, continuous location tracking, or a student-surveillance product.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A builder asks how to make smartphone-only attendance secure using biometric login, geofencing, and QR/OTP while acknowledging remaining flaws.
AnkiDroid users ask for multiple profiles on one device, showing a real need to keep distinct learners separated on shared hardware.

recurrence: The attendance request directly exposes the pressure toward intrusive controls, while the independent shared-device issue shows that learner identity and device identity are not the same.
current_workaround: Paper roll call, permanent QR codes, phone geofencing, or biometric/identity systems that collect more data than a classroom needs.
incumbents_and_gap: ClassDojo, LMS attendance modules, and geofenced check-in apps centralize student data; a teacher-controlled local check-in can record presence without pretending to prove physical identity.
smallest_useful_product: Teacher-hosted local web page generates a rotating session code; students submit a pseudonymous roster token, and the teacher exports a signed present/late/absent CSV. Non-goals: biometrics, GPS, face recognition, background tracking, or anti-cheating guarantees.
success_measure: A 30-student class completes a check-in in under two minutes, with no location or biometric fields stored and fewer than two manual corrections per session.
monetization: one-time — privacy-sensitive schools should not pay an ongoing per-student surveillance toll.
constraints: Make limitations explicit: presence of a device is not proof of attendance; encrypt roster exports; support data-retention deletion and accessible manual fallback.
why_distinct: It intentionally reduces the data and certainty claim in attendance, rather than optimizing a surveillance stack.

title: Math Textbook Margins
user: A math teacher using an interactive or PDF-based text who needs students to make predictions, sketch a step, and answer one check before receiving the next explanation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A team building an interactive CBSE math textbook says static/digital PDFs are insufficient but parents often prioritize exam-oriented outcomes over learning.
A color-blind Anki user reports that learning and filtered-card states are nearly indistinguishable, making accessibility of instructional state a concrete concern.

recurrence: The textbook maker identifies a direct static-PDF learning gap, while a separate study-tool issue shows that interactive states must remain accessible rather than communicated only by color.
current_workaround: Assign textbook/PDF pages, add separate worksheets or LMS quizzes, and rely on students to self-check after seeing worked solutions.
incumbents_and_gap: Khan Academy and commercial textbooks provide content and quizzes; lightweight classroom materials rarely let a teacher wrap any legal PDF/link with small retrieval prompts while preserving accessible state cues.
smallest_useful_product: Static web lesson wrapper: teacher supplies page links/owned excerpts and adds prediction, worked-step, and misconception prompts; students export a one-page answer record. Non-goals: textbook hosting, OCR of copyrighted PDFs, adaptive AI, or a full LMS.
success_measure: In a two-lesson pilot, 75% of students submit a prediction before revealing the worked step, and all progress states remain distinguishable without color.
monetization: free — broad classroom utility depends on working beside existing legal materials; paid template packs are optional later.
constraints: Do not host or extract copyrighted textbook content; WCAG-conscious contrast and non-color cues are mandatory; learner responses should remain exportable.
why_distinct: It adds active-recall margins around materials a teacher already has, instead of competing as another math content subscription.
